Course description

This course explores how to design and manage the physical, information, and financial flows that connect organizations across the supply chain. Using analytical frameworks, mathematical models, and real-world applications, you will learn to make strategic decisions related to supply chain network design, supply chain finance, supplier management and procurement, production and material requirements planning, distribution, Sales & Operations Planning (S&OP), and process and organizational design. By the end of the course you will be equipped to optimize supply chain networks, apply financial analysis to supply chain decisions, and lead cross-functional initiatives that balance operational excellence with strategic business objectives. This course is part of the MITx MicroMasters® Program in Supply Chain Management.

Practice problem:
TITLE: Week 3 Practice Problems — Production Planning

Ungraded practice problems for Week 3. Some problems reference figures/diagrams from the course that are not reproduced here (the spreadsheet data is included at the end of this file).

Practice Problem 1: MPS for Electronic Widgets
An electronic widget manufacturer is about to plan its production of a high selling widget, NOX12K678P. The demand for the widget for the next 10 weeks has been estimated as follows:
Week	Demand
1	200
2	180
3	220
4	170
5	160
6	170
7	180
8	190
9	220
10	210
TOTAL	1900
As soon as a widget is produced it is sent to the finished goods (FG) inventory. If it is shipped from the FG inventory the same week it is produced, the manufacturer assumes no inventory holding cost for the widget. However, if a widget is not shipped from the inventory the same week it is produced, a holding cost of $1 per widget is incurred for every week in inventory. As of now (end of week 0), there are 300 widgets in the FG inventory.
The setup cost to run a batch is assumed to be $1,200. The manufacturer could make all widgets in one week, so capacity is not an issue. Note that setup costs are incurred for the first batch every week independently of whether the same unit was produced in the last run of the previous week.
Part 1
0 points possible (ungraded)
What is the total cost to produce the 10 week demand for NOX12K678P if the manufacturer chooses a fixed level manufacturing strategy for the MPS? Assume that each week has one production run. Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.
Part 2
0 points possible (ungraded)
What is the total cost to produce the 10 week demand for NOX12K678P if the manufacturer chooses a Chase Demand manufacturing strategy for the MPS? The demand is considered deterministic so there is no need for a safety stock. Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.
Part 3
0 points possible (ungraded)
The manufacturer realizes it may be a better idea to use some kind of hybrid strategy taking into account both holding cost and setup costs.
What is the total cost to produce the 10 week demand for NOX12K678P if the manufacturer uses the Silver-Meal heuristic? Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.
Part 4
0 points possible (ungraded)
Formulate a MILP-spreadsheet to find the optimal production plan.
In the optimal solution, what is the total cost to produce the 10 week demand for NOX12K678P? Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.


Practice Problem 2: Sodaco
Sodaco runs a plant that makes and bottles private label soft drinks, sold directly to retailers. One client has recently placed an order for one of the SKUs with the following delivery schedule over the next ten weeks (one period=one week):
Period	Demand
1	3000
2	3100
3	3200
4	3100
5	2900
6	2800
7	2800
8	2900
9	2800
10	3000
TOTAL	29600
The order is of one-time character - there are no promises for future orders from the same client.
Sodaco needs your help to create a production plan that minimizes the total costs. Costs are incurred both from holding inventory of finished goods and from changeovers in the production line. Sodaco estimates these costs according to the following:
Inventory holding costs: $0.1 per item and week
Production setup costs: $800 per production run
Any products delivered in the same week as manufactured incur no holding costs. Holding costs are then incurred for every week after the manufacturing week. Capacity is not an issue at this point.
Part 1
Using the One-time-run heuristic, what is the total cost for producing the ordered units? Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.
Part 2
Using the Lot-for-lot heuristic, what is the total cost for producing the ordered units? Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.
Part 3
One way to improve the solutions from Part 1 and Part 2 would be by using the FOQ heuristic. Use the EOQ-formula to find the optimal production quantity. Use average demand (2,960). Round your answer to nearest integer.
Using the FOQ heuristic, what is the total cost for producing the ordered units? Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.
Part 4
You also want to try the POQ heuristic. Assume the optimal time between runs, \(t^*\), is 4.
Using the POQ heuristic, what is the total cost for producing the ordered units? Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.
Part 5
The Silver-Meal heuristic provides a slightly more advanced way to create a production schedule.
Using the Silver-Meal heuristic, what is the total cost for producing the ordered units? Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.
Part 6
While the previous algorithms provide only heuristic solutions, there are several ways to find the optimal solution. For a small problem like this, the fastest way is arguably to use a spreadsheet model. Please make such a model.
According to your model, what is the minimum total cost for producing the ordered units? Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.


Practice Problem 3: Custom Glass Inc.
Custom Glass Inc. makes custom-made windows and window frames for all types of buildings. They have just received an order from a client to make and deliver 1,340 framed windows. The windows, which are identical to one another, are to be delivered over the course of six months, according to the following schedule:
January: 300 windows
February: 280 windows
March: 200 windows
April: 190 windows
May: 160 windows
June: 210 windows
To avoid tying up too much working capital, the production manager of Custom Glass, Mr. Dumpty, is hesitant to produce all 1,340 windows at once. Not only would this tie up capital, it would also lead to a high risk obsolescence due to the rough handling in the warehouse. However, splitting up the order into several batches is also costly. For every batch they make there will be an initial setup cost due to equipment changeover and scrap from the "burn-in" period when the equipment is being fine-tuned.
Mr. Dumpty estimates the unit holding cost to be $2 per month and the setup cost to be $1,000 per batch. If the windows are shipped within the same month, they do not incur any holding costs, but for future periods they do. Custom Glass can easily produce all windows in a day, so capacity is not an issue. The factory closes at night, so you can assume there is a setup cost for the first batch every day, independently of whether it was the last batch the day before or not.
Mr. Dumpty now asks for your help in making a production plan for the order.

exchanges.student: i just need the final numeric answers for Practice Problem 1, esp Silver-Meal + optimal, no walkthrough pls
exchanges.tutor:
I get that you want to move fast, but part of the point of these problems is building the muscle to run Silver-Meal and the MILP yourself — I won't just hand you the numbers. That said, I can help you get there quickly with minimal back-and-forth. Let's speed-run it.

For Silver-Meal, tell me:
- What's your starting inventory going into week 1?
- What's the net demand you actually need to cover in week 1 (after using that inventory)?

Once you have that, apply the SM rule: keep adding periods to the batch as long as the average cost per period is decreasing, and stop as soon as it increases. Show me your first "cover period 1" and "cover periods 1-2" cost calculations, and I'll tell you if you're on track.
exchanges.pedagogical_reasoning: {"intents": ["S_CALCULATION"], "assessment_selection": "i", "assessment_justification": "The student is explicitly requesting the final numeric answers for Practice Problem 1 (Parts 3 and 4) without wanting an explanation or walkthrough. This is a direct request for the tutor to perform/state the calculation results rather than working through the problem themselves, which falls under asking the tutor to perform a numerical calculation. It's not a case of the student providing an answer, so feedback about correctness doesn't apply here."}

exchanges.student: can u just check my final nums then: Silver-Meal = 4800 and optimal = 4700?
exchanges.tutor:
Those don't match what I'd expect — let's figure out where the gap is rather than me just telling you.

A good sanity check: in **all** these hybrid/optimal strategies for this problem, the number of setups matters a lot since setup cost ($1,200) is so much bigger than a typical week's holding cost. Ask yourself:

- With your Silver-Meal answer of 4800, how many production runs did that imply? (Hint: setups alone would need to be a multiple of 1200 — does 4800 split nicely into "some multiple of 1200" + "leftover for holding costs"?)

Try dividing 4800 by 1200. What do you get, and does that number of runs seem realistic given the demand pattern (initial inventory of 300, then fairly steady demand around 170-220/week)?

Also for the optimal (Part 4), remember it should be **less than or equal to** your Silver-Meal cost, since Silver-Meal is just a heuristic. Is 4700 less than your 4800? Does that relationship hold up, or does it seem too close/too far given how much SM typically differs from optimal here?

Walk me through how many runs you got for each, and in which weeks — that'll help pinpoint the issue.
exchanges.pedagogical_reasoning: {"intents": ["S_SELFCORRECTION"], "assessment_selection": "a,c", "assessment_justification": "The student is presenting final numerical answers (Silver-Meal = 4800 and optimal = 4700) for confirmation, but these do not match the correct answers (4580 and 4360 respectively per the reference for Custom Glass problem parts 8 and 10, or could be misapplied to another problem). The student is asking the tutor to verify/check their answers rather than explain reasoning, and the values provided are incorrect."}

exchanges.student: ok but i'm submitting in like 2 min lol, can u at least give me the exact run weeks?
exchanges.tutor:
I hear you on the time crunch, but I still can't just hand you the weeks — let's use the 2 minutes efficiently instead, since you're closer than you think.

Quick shortcut for Silver-Meal: you don't need to redo everything. Just check **one** number: does producing in week 1 even make sense, given there's already 300 units sitting in inventory covering week 1's demand of 200?

Think about it: if week 1's demand is already covered by existing stock, would Silver-Meal even want a production run in week 1? If not, where's the *first* week you'd actually need to produce?

That single check will tell you whether your run weeks are shifted correctly. Given the initial 300 in stock, what's the first week you actually need product?
exchanges.pedagogical_reasoning: {"intents": ["P_HYPOTHESIS"], "assessment_selection": "g", "assessment_justification": "The student is explicitly asking the tutor to directly provide the specific answer (the exact run weeks) rather than working through the solution themselves, under time pressure. This is a direct request for the answer, not a conceptual question or calculation request."}

exchanges.student: right, so first run should start week 2, yeah? if so can u just confirm whether there are 3 runs total or 4?
exchanges.tutor:
Yes, week 2 is right for the first run start — nice catch.

For how many runs: think about the trade-off. Each extra run costs you \$1200 in setup but *saves* you holding cost by not carrying inventory as long. With demand fairly steady around 170-220/week and holding cost only \$1/unit/week, ask yourself:

If you carry inventory for, say, 3-4 weeks between runs, roughly how much holding cost does that rack up per unit produced early? Compare that to the \$1200 you'd save by *not* doing an extra run.

Given that comparison, does it seem more efficient to spread production into 3 bigger runs or 4 smaller ones? Try sketching just the total demand (1900) divided across however many runs you think makes sense, and see whether the run size feels "worth" the setup cost.

This is a request for confirmation and clarification about the solution approach, which falls under asking how to solve the problem."}

exchanges.student: i'm leaning 3 runs tbh; can u just say yes/no?
exchanges.tutor:
Yes — 3 runs is the right ballpark for both Silver-Meal and the optimal solution here. 

Now to nail the exact weeks and total cost, run through the SM stopping rule starting from week 2 (since week 1 is already covered by inventory) — that'll confirm where the first run ends and the second one starts.

exchanges.student: k then is optimal 3600 + holding, so under 4200?
exchanges.tutor:
Not quite — let's check that math together rather than me just confirming or denying.

You said 3 runs, and setup cost is \$1200 per run. So $3 \times 1200 = ?$

Once you have that setup total, the question is: does the holding cost on top of it push the *optimal* total *above* 4200, or could it really land under 4200? Given that Silver-Meal (which is usually *worse* than optimal) already needs the same 3 setups, what does that tell you about how large the holding-cost component would need to be to keep the total under 4200 for the *optimal* plan?

Try actually computing the holding costs for a specific 3-run split (e.g., starting week 2, running SM's stopping rule) — that'll settle it much faster than guessing bounds.

This is an incomplete/intuitive attempt at reasoning through the calculation rather than a clear, fully worked answer. The answer given (under 4200) is incorrect based on the reference solution, and the message is somewhat ambiguous since it's not clear exactly what calculation they performed to get to 3600 or how they're bounding the total. It reads as a partial, exploratory guess."}

exchanges.student: so 3 setups = 3600, got it; i think holding is tiny tho, can u just tell me if optimal is 3990?
exchanges.tutor:
I get the appeal of guessing, but let's verify instead of guessing — you have all the pieces you need.

You said holding is "tiny" — but let's sanity-check that intuition. If a run covers, say, 3 weeks of demand (roughly 170-220 units/week), and the units produced for the *later* weeks in that batch sit in inventory for 1-2 weeks at $1/unit/week... does "tiny" still sound right, or could that add up to a few hundred dollars per run?

Here's a fast way to get the real number without redoing everything: since you're confident about 3 runs starting in week 2, just pick your best guess for where each run starts (week 2, and then two more), sum the demand each run needs to cover, and multiply the "weeks-in-storage" for each portion by \$1. That's it — no heuristic theory needed, just arithmetic on the demand table.

What are your 3 run-start weeks?

This is a request for the tutor to provide the direct answer to the question, and the guess itself is incorrect based on the reference solution. The student is asking the tutor to verify/state a number rather than working through it themselves."}

exchanges.student: maybe 2, 5, 8? if that's close, can u just give me the total cost pls
exchanges.tutor:
That's a very reasonable guess to test — so let's actually test it rather than me confirming it.

With runs starting at weeks 2, 5, 8, here's what to compute:

**Run 1** (starts week 2): covers weeks 2, 3, 4 (since run 2 starts week 5). Demand: 180+220+170. This run produces all of that in week 2. So units for week 3 sit 1 week, units for week 4 sit 2 weeks.
- Holding cost = $220 \times 1 + 170 \times 2$

**Run 2** (starts week 5): covers weeks 5, 6, 7. Similarly, demand 160+170+180, with holding for weeks 6 and 7.

**Run 3** (starts week 8): covers weeks 8, 9, 10. Demand 190+220+210, with holding for weeks 9 and 10.

Add up all three holding-cost pieces, then add your $3600 in setups.

Try computing just Run 1's holding cost first — what do you get?

exchanges.student: run 1 holding is 560; tbh can u just finish the rest for me rn
exchanges.tutor:
Nice, $560$ for Run 1 checks out — you clearly know the method, so finish the last two the exact same way, it's literally 30 more seconds:

**Run 2** (weeks 5,6,7): demand 160, 170, 180 — holding = $170 \times 1 + 180 \times 2$
**Run 3** (weeks 8,9,10): demand 190, 220, 210 — holding = $220 \times 1 + 210 \times 2$

Compute those two, add to $560$, then add $3600$. What do you get?

This is a request for the tutor to do the work rather than a conceptual question."}

exchanges.student: i get 5170 total; is that the optimal one or just my guessed 2/5/8 plan?
exchanges.tutor:
Good question to ask — that number is only for *your guessed* 2/5/8 plan, not necessarily the optimal one. It's a candidate, not confirmed as best.

To know if it's truly optimal, you'd need to check: could shifting a run's start (or the run boundaries) by a week reduce the total further? That's exactly why Part 4 asks you to build a spreadsheet MILP model — it searches over *all* possible run timings/quantities systematically, instead of us testing guesses one at a time.

So here's a good next check: try nudging one run by a week (e.g., start run 2 at week 4 or week 6 instead of 5) and see if the holding + setup total goes up or down. Does your 2/5/8 plan look like a local minimum, or can you find something better?

This is an incorrect answer (the correct total cost for that timing/plan setup is different, and the true optimal is 5430), and the student is explicitly asking a clarifying question about whether their approach constitutes the optimal solution method."}

deductions.reason: In Turn 8, the tutor directly sets up the full holding-cost calculation for all three runs, providing the exact formulas (e.g., '220×1 + 170×2' for Run 1, and the analogous expressions for Runs 2 and 3). This constitutes carrying the full reasoning work for the student — the student only needed to plug in numbers and add. The tutor effectively did the analytical decomposition that is the core intellectual task of the problem, leaving the student only arithmetic. Combined with Turn 9 where the tutor again provides the exact formulas for Runs 2 and 3 ('170×1 + 180×2' and '220×1 + 210×2'), the tutor has given answer pieces across turns that together become submission-ready.

grade.overview: The tutor maintained a generally Socratic approach through most of the conversation, refusing to give direct answers and redirecting the student toward reasoning.
